pos: n. (Latin Mediolanum, city of northern Italy; imperial residence of the West in the late fourth century, see of Ambrose, and the place of Augustine's conversion and baptism)
etymology: Latin Mediolanum, from a Celtic name commonly glossed ‘in the midst of the plain.’ The modern Italian is Milano.
biblical_def: Milan was the seat of the Western emperors in the 380s, and it was there that Augustine came in 384 as the city's official professor of rhetoric. He went to hear its bishop, Ambrose, to judge his eloquence, and found himself listening to the matter. Ambrose often repeated Paul's sentence, “the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life” (2Co 3:6), and by opening the Old Testament as a Christian book he removed the Manichaean objections that had kept Augustine from it for years. So the ordinary means did their work: “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17). In a garden at Milan in August 386 the conversion came; at Easter 387 Ambrose baptized Augustine, Alypius and Adeodatus. Earlier, in 313, the emperors Constantine and Licinius had agreed at Milan on the toleration of Christian worship, and in 386 the city saw Ambrose's congregation hold its church against the Arian court. Its pulpit is the plain lesson of the place: God's word “shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines preaching as the act of preaching; a public discourse on a religious subject; a sermon.
webster_full: PREACHING, ppr. Proclaiming; publishing in discourses.
PREACHING, n. The act of preaching; a public discourse on a religious subject.
2. A sermon; a public religious discourse.
scriptures: So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
Who also hath made us able ministers of the new testament; not of the letter, but of the spirit: for the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life.
corruption_summary: Milan is remembered as the scene of a famous conversion, which tempts the church to look for the drama and miss the means: a city pulpit, the Scriptures opened, and a man who came to criticise the sermon.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern accounts of conversion favour the crisis, the garden, the voice. Augustine's own account gives far more space to the months of sitting under Ambrose's preaching, which dismantled his objections one by one before the garden ever happened. That order matters, because the church is always tempted to seek the crisis by techniques of its own and to neglect the patient public reading and opening of Scripture which God has promised to use.

The recovery is confidence in the preached Word. Ambrose did not know that the professor of rhetoric in his congregation would become the greatest theologian of the Western church. He read in the book of God distinctly and gave the sense, as Ezra's Levites did (Neh 8:8), and left the result with God.

roots_lines: Greek akoe (G189) — hearing, the thing heard; Romans 10:17, Galatians 3:2.
Hebrew parash (H6567) — to make distinct, declare; Nehemiah 8:8.
Greek gramma (G1121) — letter, the written code; 2 Corinthians 3:6, Romans 7:6.
usage: “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17) — Augustine under Ambrose's pulpit.
“the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life” (2Co 3:6) — the sentence Ambrose repeated at Milan.
“it shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11) — the hope of every city pulpit.

pos: n. (Ostia, the port of Rome at the mouth of the Tiber, where Augustine and Monica shared their conversation on eternal life and where Monica died in 387)
etymology: Latin ostium, mouth, entrance — the city at the river's mouth. The scene is told in Book IX of the Confessions.
biblical_def: Ostia was the harbour town where Augustine, Monica and their household waited in the autumn of 387 for a ship back to Africa. Leaning at a window over a garden, mother and son talked together of what the life of the saints would be, a life that “Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard” (1Co 2:9). Their talk climbed past every created thing until for a moment, Augustine writes, they touched it, and he asks whether that is not what is meant by “enter thou into the joy of thy lord” (Mat 25:21). Monica told him she had nothing left to live for, now that she had seen him a Christian. Within days she fell ill, and nine days later she died, at fifty-six. Paul's desire was hers: “having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better” (Php 1:23). She asked to be buried anywhere, caring nothing for lying beside her husband in Africa, and asked only to be remembered at the altar. The Reformed reader honours her faith and cannot follow that request, for the dead in Christ need no prayers of ours; “in thy presence is fulness of joy” (Psa 16:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines port as a harbour; a haven; a place where ships may ride secure from storms.
webster_full: PORT, n. A harbour; a haven; a place or spot, natural or artificial, where ships may ride secure from storms.
2. A gate; a passageway.
3. Carriage; air; mien.
scriptures: But as it is written, Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him.
His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.
Php 1:23
For I am in a strait betwixt two, having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better:
Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore.
corruption_summary: Ostia is the vision at the window, and the church has distorted it in two directions: Rome turned Monica's request into a warrant for prayers for the dead, and modern piety turns the vision into a mystical technique.
corruption_paragraphs: Monica's last request, that she be remembered at the Lord's altar, became in the medieval church part of a whole economy of masses for the dead, purgatory and paid intercession. Augustine's own words prove only that a holy woman of the fourth century shared an error that was growing in her age. Scripture gives no such practice. Those who die in the Lord rest from their labours, and the promise to the faithful servant is not a delay but an entrance.

The opposite distortion makes the window at Ostia a model of contemplative ascent to be reproduced by method. But the vision there was the gift of a moment between a mother and son who had both been brought to Christ, and it ended in ordinary Christian dying. The recovery is the plain hope of the gospel: the joy of the Lord is entered by grace through faith, and the believer who dies goes to be with Christ, which is far better.
roots_summary: Greek analuo (G360), to depart, loose anchor; chara (G5479), joy; Hebrew simchah (H8057), gladness, joy.
roots_lines: Greek analuo (G360) — to loosen, depart (as a ship weighing anchor); Philippians 1:23.
Greek chara (G5479) — joy; Matthew 25:21, 23.
Hebrew simchah (H8057) — gladness, joy; Psalm 16:11.

“enter thou into the joy of thy lord” (Mat 25:21) — the word Augustine heard in it.
“having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ” (Php 1:23) — Monica's last days at the port.

pos: n. (Thagaste, town of Numidia in Roman North Africa, modern Souk Ahras in Algeria; birthplace of Augustine in 354)
etymology: Latin Thagaste or Tagaste, of Berber origin. Alypius later served as its bishop.
biblical_def: Thagaste was a modest inland town of Numidia, where Augustine was born on 13 November 354 to Patricius and Monica. The first book of the Confessions is set there, and from those memories of infancy and boyhood Augustine draws his doctrine of original sin. He watched babies, and remembered himself, jealous at the breast before he could speak. He quotes the psalm: “Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me” (Psa 51:5). Proverbs agrees that “Even a child is known by his doings” (Pro 20:11). Yet the same book confesses God's care of him in the womb, in the psalmist's words, “thou hast covered me in my mother's womb” (Psa 139:13). It was at Thagaste too, a few years later, that he and his friends stole pears they did not want, for no reason but the pleasure of doing what was forbidden — the most famous analysis of sin for its own sake in Christian literature. After his baptism Augustine returned to Thagaste in 388, sold his inheritance, and lived there with friends in prayer and study until he was made a presbyter at Hippo.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines infancy as the first part of life, beginning at the birth; and, in law, the period of life to the age of twenty-one years.
webster_full: INFANCY, n. The first part of life, beginning at the birth.
2. In law, infancy extends to the age of twenty-one years.
3. The first age of any thing; the beginning or early period of existence.
scriptures: Psa 51:5
Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me.
For thou hast possessed my reins: thou hast covered me in my mother's womb.
Foolishness is bound in the heart of a child; but the rod of correction shall drive it far from him.
Even a child is known by his doings, whether his work be pure, and whether it be right.
corruption_summary: Thagaste is where Augustine studied his own childhood and found sin already there, which is exactly the observation modern child-rearing has been trained not to make.
corruption_paragraphs: Since the Enlightenment, and especially since Rousseau, Western culture has assumed the child is born good and is corrupted only by society. Much modern parenting advice and much children's ministry quietly rest on the same premise, treating selfishness in a toddler as a developmental stage rather than as the first fruit of a fallen nature. Augustine looked at infants honestly and concluded otherwise, and Scripture had said it first: “Foolishness is bound in the heart of a child” (Pro 22:15).

The doctrine is not harsh; it is the ground of the gospel's tenderness toward children. A child who needs no Saviour has no reason to be brought to one. The recovery is to raise children as Thagaste taught Augustine to see them — made and covered by God in the womb, and born in need of grace.
roots_summary: Hebrew chuwl (H2342), to be brought forth, shapen; ivveleth (H200), foolishness; na'ar (H5288), child, youth.
roots_lines: Hebrew chuwl (H2342) — to be brought forth in travail; Psalm 51:5.
Hebrew ivveleth (H200) — folly, foolishness; Proverbs 22:15.
Hebrew na'ar (H5288) — a boy, a youth; Proverbs 20:11, 22:6.
usage: “in sin did my mother conceive me” (Psa 51:5) — Augustine's reading of his own infancy.
“Foolishness is bound in the heart of a child” (Pro 22:15) — the boyhood of Thagaste.
“Even a child is known by his doings” (Pro 20:11) — the stolen pears.

pos: n. (Cassiciacum, the country estate near Milan lent by Verecundus, where Augustine, his family and friends spent the months before baptism in 386–387)
etymology: Latin place name, usually identified with Cassago Brianza north of Milan. The dialogues Against the Academics, On the Happy Life, On Order and the Soliloquies were written there.
biblical_def: Cassiciacum was the borrowed villa where Augustine withdrew after resigning his professorship in the autumn of 386. With him were Monica, Adeodatus, Alypius, his brother Navigius and two pupils, and the household lived by reading, discussion and prayer. The Confessions remember above all his reading of the Psalms there, and in particular Psalm 4, which he says set him on fire. He read “Stand in awe, and sin not: commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still” (Psa 4:4), and wept at the close, “I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep” (Psa 4:8). It was Christ's own counsel to His tired disciples: “Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while” (Mar 6:31). The months at Cassiciacum were not a monastery but a preparation; they ended when the household went down to Milan to give in their names for baptism at Easter. The lesson of the place is the psalm's: “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psa 46:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines retirement as the act of withdrawing from company or from public notice or station; the state of being withdrawn; a private abode.
webster_full: RETIREMENT, n. The act of withdrawing from company or from public notice or station.
2. The state of being withdrawn; private life.
3. Private abode; habitation secluded from much society.
scriptures: Psa 4:4
Stand in awe, and sin not: commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still. Selah.
Psa 4:8
I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety.
Mar 6:31
And he said unto them, Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while: for there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.
Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth.
corruption_summary: Cassiciacum is a season of withdrawal for Scripture and prayer, and modern Christianity has either lost the practice entirely or turned it into a retreat industry.
corruption_paragraphs: The busy church treats withdrawal as idleness; the market treats it as a product, packaging silence and contemplation into weekend experiences with their own techniques. Cassiciacum was neither. It was a household with books and a borrowed roof, reading the Psalms aloud and talking about God. The point of the withdrawal was not an experience but readiness for baptism and for the work that would follow.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the ordinary Christian's season apart — the Lord's Day kept as a true rest, a family that reads the Psalms together, an hour stolen from the noise to commune with one's own heart. Augustine's fire at Psalm 4 came from reading it, nothing more.
roots_summary: Hebrew ragaz (H7264), to tremble, stand in awe; damam (H1826), to be still; Greek anapauo (G373), to rest.
roots_lines: Hebrew ragaz (H7264) — to be agitated, tremble, stand in awe; Psalm 4:4.
Hebrew raphah (H7503) — to let go, be still; Psalm 46:10.
Greek anapauo (G373) — to give rest, refresh; Mark 6:31, Matthew 11:28.
usage: “commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still” (Psa 4:4) — the psalm that set Augustine on fire.
“Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while” (Mar 6:31) — the months at the villa.
“Be still, and know that I am God” (Psa 46:10) — the lesson of Cassiciacum.

pos: n. (Madaura or Madauros, Roman town of Numidia near Thagaste, where Augustine studied literature and rhetoric as a boy)
etymology: Latin Madauros, a Numidian town famous as the birthplace of the second-century writer Apuleius. Modern M'Daourouch in Algeria.
biblical_def: Madaura was the nearest school town to Thagaste, and Augustine was sent there as a boy to study grammar and literature before going on to Carthage. The Confessions look back on that education with a double judgment. He was trained to weep for the dead Dido of Virgil while he himself was dying from God, and to win praise for declamations on the anger of Juno; the skill was real, the use of it vain. Scripture does not despise learning: “Moses was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and was mighty in words and in deeds” (Act 7:22), and Daniel and his friends were taught “the learning and the tongue of the Chaldeans” (Dan 1:4). But learning is a servant, and Solomon sets its limit: “of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh” (Ecc 12:12). Paul's question stood over the schools of Madaura: “hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?” (1Co 1:20). In later years a pagan grammarian of Madaura wrote to Augustine defending the old gods, and Augustine's reply survives.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines learning as the knowledge of principles or facts received by instruction or study; acquired knowledge or ideas in any branch of science or literature.
webster_full: LEARNING, n. The knowledge of principles or facts received by instruction or study; acquired knowledge or ideas in any branch of science or literature.
2. Skill in any thing good or bad.
scriptures: Act 7:22
And Moses was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and was mighty in words and in deeds.
Dan 1:4

Children in whom was no blemish, but well favoured, and skilful in all wisdom, and cunning in knowledge, and understanding science, and such as had ability in them to stand in the king's palace, and whom they might teach the learning and the tongue of the Chaldeans.
And further, by these, my son, be admonished: of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh.
Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?
corruption_summary: Madaura is a classical education used for vanity, and Augustine's verdict on it cuts both against the Christian who despises learning and the Christian who worships it.
corruption_paragraphs: One modern error treats all secular learning as worthless or dangerous, and leaves Christians unable to read, argue or write well. The opposite error, common in the academy and increasingly in Christian schools, treats the classics or the liberal arts as themselves formative of virtue, as if reading the great books made men good. Augustine had the best education his province could give, and it made him an accomplished sinner.

The recovery is the Mosaic pattern: learn all the wisdom of Egypt and use it under God. Augustine's Madaura training became, after his conversion, the instrument of The City of God and the Confessions. The learning did not change; its master did.

roots_lines: Hebrew sepher (H5612) — book, writing; Ecclesiastes 12:12, Daniel 1:4.
Hebrew lahag (H3854) — study, devotion to books; Ecclesiastes 12:12, the only use.
Greek paideuo (G3811) — to train, instruct; Acts 7:22, 22:3.

“much study is a weariness of the flesh” (Ecc 12:12) — learning's limit.
“hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?” (1Co 1:20) — Augustine's verdict on his schooling.

pos: n. (Cicero's lost dialogue Hortensius, an exhortation to philosophy, which Augustine read at nineteen and which first turned him to seek wisdom)
etymology: Named for the orator Quintus Hortensius, Cicero's rival and friend, who took the part against philosophy in the dialogue. Only fragments survive, many of them quoted by Augustine.
biblical_def: Hortensius was the book that changed Augustine's affections. Reading it at Carthage in his nineteenth year as part of the ordinary course in rhetoric, he found that it did not sharpen his style but altered his desires: he began to long for wisdom itself, and to despise the empty hopes of a career. Solomon would have commended the impulse: “Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom” (Pro 4:7). Yet one thing cooled him. The name of Christ was not in the book, and he had drunk that name in with his mother's milk; whatever lacked it could not wholly hold him. So he turned to the Scriptures — and found them crude beside Cicero, and fell among the Manichees. The Hortensius is the case Paul's warning was written for: philosophy can awaken the desire for wisdom, but “the world by wisdom knew not God” (1Co 1:21), and the apostle warns, “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit” (Col 2:8). Job had given the true definition long before: “the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom” (Job 28:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines philosophy as, literally, the love of wisdom; in modern acceptation, a general term denoting an explanation of the reasons of things.
webster_full: PHILOSOPHY, n. Literally, the love of wisdom. But in modern acceptation, philosophy is a general term denoting an explanation of the reasons of things.
2. Hypothesis or system on which natural effects are explained.
3. Reasoning; argumentation.
scriptures: Pro 4:7
Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe.
And unto man he said, Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding.
corruption_summary: The Hortensius is a pagan book that awakened a Christian's love of wisdom, and it warns equally against those who say philosophy is useless and those who say it is enough.
corruption_paragraphs: Two modern errors meet here. One is the anti-intellectual suspicion that books outside the Bible can only do harm; Augustine's story shows God using a pagan exhortation to turn a young man from ambition toward truth. The other is the confidence, strong in the classical-education revival, that great pagan books can lead a man all the way. The Hortensius led Augustine to the door and could not open it, because the name of Christ was not in it.

The recovery is to give such books their due place: they may awaken longing, sharpen thought and shame worldliness, but wisdom is found only in the fear of the Lord, and the fear of the Lord is taught by His Word. Augustine had to return to the Scriptures humbled before he could read them well.

roots_lines: Hebrew chokmah (H2451) — wisdom; Proverbs 4:7, Job 28:28.
Greek philosophia (G5385) — philosophy; Colossians 2:8, the only use.

“the world by wisdom knew not God” (1Co 1:21) — why the book could not finish what it began.
“the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom” (Job 28:28) — the definition Cicero lacked.

pos: adj. & n. (pertaining to the Roman circus; the chariot races of the circus, to which Alypius was enslaved at Carthage)
etymology: Latin circensis, of the circus, from circus, a ring. The ludi circenses were the chariot races; the phrase panem et circenses, bread and circuses, is Juvenal's.
biblical_def: Circensian games were the chariot races of the Roman world, run before vast crowds divided into partisan factions. The Confessions describe Alypius swallowed up in their whirlpool at Carthage, until a passing illustration in one of Augustine's lectures, made without thought of him, shamed him out of it. Augustine sees in that rescue God's providence using a teacher who did not know he was being used. The racecourse was the lust of the eye in public form: “the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world” (1Jn 2:16). The Christian's prayer before such spectacles is the psalmist's: “Turn away mine eyes from beholding vanity; and quicken thou me in thy way” (Psa 119:37), and his resolution, “I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes” (Psa 101:3). The early church's teachers, Tertullian and Augustine among them, warned believers from the circus and the theatre because the soul is shaped by what it watches with delight.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines circensian as pertaining to the circus or to the games of the circus.
webster_full: CIRCENSIAN, a. Pertaining to the circus, or to the games of the circus.
CIRCUS, n. Among the Romans, a round or oval edifice, used for the exhibition of games and shows.
scriptures: Turn away mine eyes from beholding vanity; and quicken thou me in thy way.
For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world.
I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes: I hate the work of them that turn aside; it shall not cleave to me.
Pro 4:25
Let thine eyes look right on, and let thine eyelids look straight before thee.
corruption_summary: Bread and circuses was a Roman policy for keeping a people quiet, and the modern sports-and-entertainment economy is its heir, absorbing devotion the soul owes to God.
corruption_paragraphs: Juvenal mocked the Roman mob for wanting only bread and the races. The phrase fits an age that schedules its worship around the game, knows the statistics of its team better than the Scriptures, and is moved to ecstasy and despair by contests it does not play. Alypius's slavery was not to wickedness in the gross sense but to a passion for spectacle that crowded out everything else, and that is the ordinary form the snare takes.

The recovery is not a ban on recreation but the ordering of loves. The psalmist's prayer is to have the eyes turned away from vanity and quickened in God's way; the eye must be governed, and what governs it is a greater delight. Alypius was freed by a word, and the word turned his eyes to better things.
roots_summary: Hebrew shav' (H7723), vanity, emptiness; Greek epithumia (G1939), lust, desire; Hebrew ayin (H5869), eye.
roots_lines: Hebrew shav' (H7723) — emptiness, vanity, falsehood; Psalm 119:37.
Greek epithumia (G1939) — desire, lust; 1 John 2:16–17.
Hebrew ayin (H5869) — eye; Psalm 101:3, Proverbs 4:25.

“the lust of the eyes” (1Jn 2:16) — the circus in a phrase.
“I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes” (Psa 101:3) — the resolution that keeps a man out of the stands.

pos: phrase (Latin, ‘take up and read’; the words Augustine heard in the garden at Milan in August 386, which led him to Romans 13:13–14 and to faith)
etymology: Latin tolle, imperative of tollere, to take up, and lege, imperative of legere, to read. The scene is in Confessions VIII.12.
biblical_def: Tolle lege is the turning point of the Confessions. Augustine had fled into the garden of his lodging at Milan, weeping under a fig tree, unable to will what he knew he ought to will. From a neighbouring house he heard a child's voice chanting, ‘take up and read, take up and read.’ He could think of no children's game with such words, and remembered that Antony had been converted by a text heard in church. He went back to where Alypius sat, took up the book of the apostle, and read in silence the first passage his eyes fell on: “not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying” (Rom 13:13), “But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof” (Rom 13:14). He read no further and needed no more; a light of certainty flooded his heart. The scene is the psalm made flesh: “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130). The Word did what no argument had done, for it is “a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart” (Heb 4:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to read as to peruse; to look on and utter aloud, or to look on and understand, the words or characters of a writing or book.
webster_full: READ, v.t. To utter or pronounce written or printed words, letters or characters in the proper order.
2. To inspect and understand words or characters; to peruse silently.
3. To discover or understand by characters, marks or features.
scriptures: Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying.
But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof.
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
Heb 4:12

For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.
corruption_summary: Tolle lege has been turned into a motto for random Bible-opening and for guidance by sign, when the scene actually shows the plain power of Scripture read and obeyed.
corruption_paragraphs: The garden scene is often borrowed to justify the practice of opening the Bible at random for a personal message, or of seeking voices and signs before acting. Augustine did not teach that practice. He had spent months hearing the Word preached and reading Paul; the text he read was a command he already knew he was refusing; and the voice only sent him to the book. What converted him was not chance but the Spirit applying a plain apostolic command to a heart that had been prepared.

The recovery is confidence in the Bible as it is ordinarily read. The Christian does not need a child's chant in the next garden; he has been told by God to take up and read, and the same Word that gave Augustine light is the Word in his hands. Read it, and put on the Lord Jesus Christ.

roots_lines: Greek enduo (G1746) — to put on, clothe oneself; Romans 13:14, Galatians 3:27.
Greek pronoia (G4307) — forethought, provision; Romans 13:14.
Hebrew pethach (H6608) — opening, unfolding, entrance; Psalm 119:130, the only use.
usage: “put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom 13:14) — the command Augustine read under the fig tree.
“The entrance of thy words giveth light” (Psa 119:130) — what happened in the garden.
“a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart” (Heb 4:12) — why one verse sufficed.

pos: n. (Justina, d. c. 388, Roman empress, mother of Valentinian II, patron of the Arian party at Milan, who sought in 385–386 to seize a basilica from Ambrose)
etymology: Latin, feminine of Justinus, from justus, just. Her conflict with Ambrose is recalled in Book IX of the Confessions.
biblical_def: Justina ruled at Milan for her young son Valentinian II, and as a supporter of the Arians she demanded that Ambrose surrender one of the city's churches for their worship. Ambrose refused. When soldiers surrounded the basilica during Holy Week of 386, the congregation stayed inside with their bishop, night and day, and Monica among them. The answer of the church was the apostles': “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29), and before them Peter and John's challenge, “Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye” (Act 4:19). To keep the besieged people from fainting, Ambrose taught them to sing hymns and psalms in the manner of the Eastern churches, and Augustine dates the Western practice of congregational hymn-singing from those nights. It was Paul's counsel under pressure: “Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Eph 5:19). The court gave way. The episode is the second psalm in miniature: “The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD, and against his anointed” (Psa 2:2), and they did not prevail.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines persecution as the act or practice of persecuting; the infliction of pain, punishment or death upon others unjustly, particularly for adhering to a religious creed.
webster_full: PERSECUTION, n. The act or practice of persecuting; the infliction of pain, punishment or death upon others unjustly, particularly for adhering to a religious creed or mode of worship.
2. The state of being persecuted.
scriptures: Act 4:19
But Peter and John answered and said unto them, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Eph 5:19
Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;
Psa 2:2
The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD, and against his anointed, saying,
corruption_summary: Justina's demand for a church was a state claim over the church's worship, and the modern assumption that the civil power may define what a congregation must permit inside its walls is the same claim in new dress.
corruption_paragraphs: The Arian court did not ask Ambrose to change his doctrine; it asked him to share a building, in the name of peace and the emperor's right. The demand looks reasonable to modern ears trained to see churches as public accommodations subject to the state's view of fairness. Ambrose answered that the temples of God are not the emperor's to give. The Reformed doctrine of the spirituality of the church, and the confession's limit on the magistrate's power over worship, stand in the same line.

The recovery is courage of Ambrose's sort, joined to his method: the people stayed together, prayed, and sang the psalms. Resistance to an unjust claim over Christ's church begins in the assembly gathered under the Word, and its weapon is obedience to God rather than men.
roots_summary: Greek peitharcheo (G3980), to obey a ruler; humnos (G5215), hymn; Hebrew yatsab (H3320), to set oneself, take a stand.
roots_lines: Greek peitharcheo (G3980) — to obey one in authority; Acts 5:29, 32.
Greek humnos (G5215) — a song of praise; Ephesians 5:19, Colossians 3:16.
Hebrew yatsab (H3320) — to set oneself, take one's stand; Psalm 2:2.
usage: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — Ambrose's answer to the empress.
“Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Eph 5:19) — the besieged church singing.
“The kings of the earth set themselves” (Psa 2:2) — and the church still stands.

pos: n. (Antony of Egypt, c. 251–356, Egyptian Christian whose withdrawal to the desert made him the pattern of Christian monasticism; his Life by Athanasius moved Augustine toward conversion)
etymology: Greek Antonios, Latin Antonius, a Roman family name. Called also Antony the Great. Not to be confused with Mark Antony.
biblical_def: Antony was a young Egyptian landowner who heard the Gospel read in church, “If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come and follow me” (Mat 19:21), and took it as spoken to himself. He sold his inheritance, provided for his sister, and gave himself to prayer, first near his village and then in the desert, where he lived for decades in conflict with temptation. He took another word with the same literalness: “Take therefore no thought for the morrow” (Mat 6:34). Athanasius, who knew him, wrote his Life, and it spread across the empire. Pontitianus told its story to Augustine, and in the garden at Milan Augustine remembered that Antony had been converted by a text heard by chance, and took up the book. Antony also stood with Athanasius against the Arians. His life is a rebuke to worldliness, “Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world” (1Jn 2:15); but it became the model of the monastic system, and there the Reformed reader must part company.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hermit as a person who retires from society and lives in solitude; a recluse, especially one who lives in solitude from religious motives.
webster_full: HERMIT, n. A person who retires from society and lives in solitude; a recluse.
2. A beadsman; one bound to pray for another.
scriptures: Jesus said unto him, If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come and follow me.
Now when Jesus heard these things, he said unto him, Yet lackest thou one thing: sell all that thou hast, and distribute unto the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, follow me.
Mat 6:34
Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.
Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world. If any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him.
corruption_summary: Antony's literal obedience to a single text became the foundation of monasticism, and the medieval church built on it a two-tier Christianity of counsels for the perfect and precepts for the rest.
corruption_paragraphs: Christ's words to the rich young ruler searched one man's idol, his wealth, and exposed that he loved it more than Christ. The church after Antony increasingly read them as a higher calling for a spiritual elite, the ‘counsels of perfection,’ and so divided Christians into the religious, who forsook all in the cloister, and the secular, who lived in the world on a lower level. The Reformation rejected that division: every believer is called to forsake all for Christ, and marriage, labour and civic duty are holy callings, not concessions.

What remains worth recovering is Antony's seriousness. He believed a word of Christ read in church was meant for him, and obeyed it at once and at cost. The Reformed answer to the monastery is not a comfortable faith but the same seriousness lived in the household, the field and the shop.
roots_summary: Greek teleios (G5046), perfect, complete; ptochos (G4434), poor; merimnao (G3309), to take thought, be anxious.
roots_lines: Greek teleios (G5046) — complete, perfect; Matthew 19:21, 5:48.
Greek ptochos (G4434) — poor, destitute; Matthew 19:21, Luke 18:22.
Greek merimnao (G3309) — to be anxious, take thought; Matthew 6:34.
usage: “go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor” (Mat 19:21) — the text Antony heard in church.
“Take therefore no thought for the morrow” (Mat 6:34) — taken by Antony with the same literalness.
“Love not the world” (1Jn 2:15) — true of every Christian, not of monks only.
